item.title: How do I meet people?
item.description:
When contemplating various outings—to conferences, to parties an hour’s drive away in San Francisco, to ecstatic dances, to old friends’ brunches—a consideration that arises is “it’s good to meet people”.

It seems helpful then to know, how do I actually meet people? (And perhaps, how do you actually meet people?)

To that end, here are ten ways I became friends with people (not exclusively the closest), emojified to help with seeing patterns:

  1. Perhaps we met in the Future of Humanity Institute office. The period of knowing each other better began with a party at my house and continued through regular messaging, living together and dating. 🫶(⟡) : 🥳☎️🏠🌹
  2. We met somehow through Effective Altruism somewhere before 2012 (probably also in the vicinity of the FHI office) then got to know each other better through living together, work collaboration and intentional hanging out. 🫶(⟡) : 🏠👷‍♀️☎️
  3. I wrote to them about their dating doc, and we got to know each other through going on an extended first date, then keeping in touch and not dating, then dating. 🌹: ☎️🌹
  4. We met so we could consider each other as potential housemates, thanks to a friend’s recommendation. We got to know each other well as housemates. 🏠👭 : 🏠
  5. Someone put us in touch for me to talk about them contributing to AI safety. Our closer acquaintance began with talking when I was visiting the FHI office. We got to know each other well through social calls, a brief period of dates, then living together. 👷‍♀️ : ⟡☎️🌹🏠
  6. We probably met as housemates, and got to know each other living together in another house and working together. 🏠 : 🏠👷‍♀️
  7. Our first conversation was about whether they might want to work for me, which they didn’t. We got to know each other well through living together, regular calls, and dating. 👷‍♀️ : 🏠☎️🌹
  8. We probably met through Effective Altruism events somehow an incredibly long time ago, and got to know each other better through mutual friends, living together, and one-on-one hangouts. 🫶 : 👭🏠☎️
  9. The first meeting I remember was because our then-partners were best friends—the four of us went out for dinner. Both relationships ended soon after, but we got close via coworking with other mutual friends, then perhaps more so from living together. 👭 : 👷‍♀️🏠
  10. We met when I intentionally moved into the house where he lived in order to meet interesting people, then spent the month hanging out a large fraction of the time. We did get to know each other even better through dating, but we already knew each other pretty well by that point. 🏠 : 🏠🌹

Tally of how I got to know people:

First meetings:

  • 🫶 Effective Altruist and/or AI risk social spaces: 3
  • 🏠 Housemates: 3
  • 👷‍♀️ Job duties: 2 (I separate this from ‘job related socializing’, partly to encourage myself to do my job duties—beyond whatever importance they have, sometimes they lead me to meet new close friends!)
  • 👭 Mutual friends: 2
  • 🌹 Romance: 1

Getting close:

  • 🏠 Living together: 9
  • 🌹 Romance: 5
  • ☎️ Frequent correspondence or organized hangouts: 6
  • 👷‍♀️ Job duties: 3
  • 🥳 Parties: 1 (though surely I’m missing some in the ‘vaguely through EA’ category, and probably between some first meetings and some knowing each other betters)
  • 👭 Mutual friends: 1

Extra:

  • ⟡ FHI involved somehow: 3

Takeaways:

  • Hell yeah group houses! Living with people seems to be super important for strengthening relationships (or else when I’m going to try to be close to someone anyway, I manage to finagle living with them, which seems at least a bit true).
  • I was going to infer that parties seem fine to miss, but even that single 1 is incredibly precious to me so I should probably go to more parties on reconsideration.
  • Romance is a great source of friendships for me, but I’m unusually good at being friends with exes for some reason.
  • Job duties: great
  • I met half of these people initially through projects and none through parties—this at least suggests that if people are saying I should go to a party in SF to meet people I’ve never met before, I might do better to stay at home and work, even from a meeting people perspective (assuming working at home will lead to meeting people later, e.g. when I finish and share the work).
  • This is harder than I expected! For instance, I didn’t list ‘through AI safety’ much, so you might infer that doing AI safety is not an awesome way to meet people. However beyond the clear connections between working on AI safety and being at EA events or in the FHI office, my housemates and romantic partners are very likely to be working on AI safety. So is working on AI safety actually required for any of these meetings? My guess is no, this is mostly from common causes—but in general, the causal situation seems complicated.
  • The end of FHI may impact my social life more than I realized

How do you meet people?

item.title: Representation of Consequences
item.description:
Impossible knowledge and the real world

Human knowledge of the real world is imagined or remembered in symbols (or codes such as language) or in sensory representations.

Some real-world knowledge implies your impossible presence in that time, place, or situation.

Lets consider a few examples:

  • The surface of the sun: the sight blinds you, your presence near there incinerates you, it’s not an embodied possibility for you to go there and see it. But if you don’t conceptualize it in words or text or a symbol for the referent of surface of the sun, you “see it”, don’t you? Maybe even up close. You could hear it as well, through the instruments letting you process its presence. Maybe it feels warm from far away. What does it look like up close to you?
  • A time 500 years ago: a place that you cannot visit because it existed during a time before you were born. No matter how accurate a representation of it you happen to imagine in your mind, you have never genuinely been there. But we can all imagine that place, people speaking an older dialect in some castle or village, lit by torches at night, throwing their slop out of their windows in the morning, carts being dragged through the streets, peasants hawking wares. Or something similar.
  • Someone else’s life: you might know them well, and have witnessed exactly what happened to them, but you were not that person at that time. You were you. Yet in your mind, you experienced the feelings they had, and understood the situation as them. For example, you watched them get married and felt a bit of their happiness. Yay!
  • Your life experienced differently in hindsight: you are yourself and you were yourself then but your idea of it now is not purely a memory of experience. Most memories are a construct, an imagination, a reconstruction combining memory and narrative, some of it new. That time you got really mad, oh it was no big deal, really. Sure. The big bang? You weren’t atoms yet. That time you left the front door open? Nope, it didn’t happen that way. Swimming alone in the ocean? There are sharks there so good luck with that. The primordial void. Yeah, what’s that like? That influencer’s perfect life? Why, that is your picture there! You remember how you took it.

What am I trying to say? It’s not our potential for inaccurate representation , it’s not the power of our imagination, it’s not our need for instruments to extend our senses, it’s not our use of digital media, AI or each other. It’s that every idea that is not a mere language description is also represented in the senses as if you are there experiencing that then. But you are not there in a lot(most) of the ideas as you represent them to yourself.

In fact, some ideas are categorically impossible to experience as we represent them, because in that actual situation we represent, we lack all means of experience. This fundamental epistemological hurdle is difficult to appreciate. It has stark implications.

In short: The problem for us humans is that no matter what we try to describe in specific terms, we have to imagine it as if (at least one of) our senses are processing it, that is, as if we are experiencing it. However, as my examples illustrate, for one reason or another, that is impossible. We are not eternal or omni-present or invincible.

Human action and what doesn’t happen

Causes converge in our experience from the past to the present. The present carries on, a single point of convergence. Causes do not diverge among possible futures in our experience. Instead, we follow a single path among them, calling any other paths “possible” if we believe so. The only future we don’t have to believe in is the one that the present starts and that is because we are experiencing it as it happens.

We ourselves take action in the present. Our actions are all physical movements, including speech. Our lungs squeeze air through the vocal cords, creating air vibrations that resonate in our throats and skulls.

Using physical movements, we act on the world, intervening in our world and causing consequences in the present. Through our movements we intervene in the lives of others, making ourselves causes of (or at least contributing factors to) their experience. Without movements by us, other causes determine what happens next.

Here are some examples:

  • You push a wooden door open. Behind the door is a person standing still. The door bumps her head. She yells, “Hey!”
  • A butterfly brushes a dog’s face. The dog’s eyeballs follow the butterfly’s movements while the dog’s head stays still.
  • A man crosses a crosswalk while looking at the red walk sign in front of him. A driver presses her brake pedal and narrows her eyes at the man as he continues walking. Another driver presses down on his brake pedal in the car to her right.
  • A boy’s index finger hits the Enter key on the keyboard and he sighs. He sits still for a minute, breathing slowly, and his facial muscles extend. Then the hammer hits the inside of the bell on the wall and the boy stands up from his seat.
  • A bottle sits on a table. The visitors watch the bottle as someone else seated at the table grabs the bottle and moves it across the table. Then their eyes look at the person sitting in front of the bottle.
  • Two people talk to each other as they sit at a bench. Their voices raise and one of them retrieves a phone from her pocket. Another person sitting at the bench stares straight ahead.

It’s not when or whether counterfactual futures are possible. It’s not that refraining from action is or is not a cause in itself. It’s not that accountability depends on intent in addition to personal movement. It’s not whether there are parallel universes. It’s not about a future of causing consequences using brain-sensing devices. It’s not about free will. It’s that imagining the cost of choosing one future over another involves conceptualizing about and believing in at least one future that doesn’t happen.

The absent futures in an opportunity cost calculation, when seen in retrospect, are the ones whose presence we still attribute to a set of causes even though the futures did not happen. Remember, our belief in any non-occurring future and its causes has either a symbolic or an impossible sensory representation in our heads (see Part I). Intuitively, then, any regret or relief that we humans experience depends on at least one of those categories of representation.

Imagining, moving and matching

Regardless of when and where you imagine an event, your empirical knowledge can only be about, at most, the world around you that you sense directly (for example, what you hear someone saying nearby). Or if even that information is in error (for example, if you are wearing noise-silencing earphones), then memory of sensory experience is all the empirical knowledge you have.

Can memory tell you about the present?

Of course it can, provided that the environment you remember is similar to the environment that surrounds you now. However, if you never determine that a pattern is present, you remain ignorant of its presence in your experience when it is there.

Here are some examples of basic human pattern detection:

  • You notice an increase in humidity at the far end of the kitchen by the stove. In fact, a housemate made pasta and left a cloud of vapor behind after they cleaned up the mess. You assume the same because you make a vapor cloud there when you make spaghetti.
  • You hear a noise like a loud motor echoing outside, lasting for several hours in the early morning. It repeats every night for days and has no visible source. In fact, someone is running a generator inside their enclosed yard. You suspect it’s night construction happening on the freeway a few blocks away.
  • You see a person dressed in costume walking down your street and carrying a trumpet. Several people follow, all in costume. In fact, these people are going to a protest. However, you assume that they are going to some costume party.
  • You see a soda can on the table. You expect that the can will feel like a cylinder when you grab it. To your surprise, your fingers find a small one-finger suction cup handle attached to the other side. You take a drink, expecting cold soda water, but the can contains coffee.

Remembering that we imagine impossible sensory experiences and that we move in the world to intervene in it, our inference process includes:

  • Imagining (impossible) sensory experiences.
  • Moving our bodies.
  • Matching (nonexistent) patterns using our senses.

It’s not that human function is conceptually simple. It’s not that matching is inference. It’s not that an individual’s sensory experiences provide little information about the world. It’s not that memory is insufficient or that imagination is essential or that imagination is built from memory and more imagination. It’s not that symbolization translates from sensory experiences or that imagination is limited to sense representations or infers one representation from another. It’s not that the world shows lots of regularity through time or space. It’s that we create or understand our consequences for everything through a process that includes imagining, moving and matching.

Humans are ignorant

If you are human, then (you can assume) movement creates your consequences, pattern-matching is how you infer about consequences, and imagination lets you represent consequences to yourself. As an agent in the world, you understand patterns prospectively. You never actually know what the truth is, but embedded in a civilization that inputs information to your senses, you adopt ideas of it.

Here are some examples:

  • You see a weight plate at the gym. The label says “50”, as in 50 pounds. You grab it by the handle and it lifts easily. When you weigh it on the bathroom scale, you decide it weighs closer to 10 pounds.
  • You receive a call from your partner. The urgency in her voice suggests an important problem. Her words, “We are out of toilet paper” suggest differently. You agree to pick some up on the way home.
  • Your favorite web show is cancelled. You check the youtube channel, and find a good-bye video. You watch it tearfully. Two days later, the youtube homepage shows a new video from the same channel. How quickly things change!
  • In the morning before you shower, you discover what looks like a rash on your elbow. You take a picture of it on your phone. In the evening, you inspect your arm in front of the bathroom mirror and you don’t see a rash anymore. Still concerned, you send the picture of the rash to your doctor. The doctor says you slept on your elbow strangely and did not have a rash on your elbow.
  • To calculate a metric at work, you consider data from a specific data set. During your performance review, you discover that your metrics do not match what your boss reviewed all year, another set of related metrics based on [narrower data].

It’s not that you rely on evidence. It’s not that some interpretations are better than others or better informed than others. It’s not that you rely on other’s findings for your own beliefs. It’s not that you argue from ignorance, rely on a closed world assumption, or put the burden of proof on one presumption or another. It’s not that different experiences tell you different information or that observation, education, or imitation also shape your knowledge.

It is that you are trapped in the outputs of your sensory experience and imagination and so you cannot know the truth no matter what your inference capabilities and accumulated knowledge. Knowledge of non-provisional, non-speculative, actual truth is reserved for mythical omniscient omnipotents, Gods. And you are not such a god.

Your lack of omniscience guarantees your lack of omnipotence. An ignorant omnipotent does not know their consequences and so does not control what exists. You do qualify as ignorant. You are not an uncertain god. You are an ignorant being. Everyone is.

NOTE: For this cross-post to less wrong, I copied over my own written post from elsewhere. It's not terribly important to you, I imagine, but I wrote this all myself. It is written for humans and for AI, since both have been readers of mine in the past. That is the reason why the writing style and pacing might seem a bit strange to you. But it works for me, so yeah. As for why I wrote it, my experiences and education in the real world taught me that we all learn from experience.

This post proposes a fundamental descriptive or observational model that motivates why we humans perform presumptive reasoning, rely on abduction, inversion, implication, and arguments from ignorance, and think in (implicit) analogies as part of relying on experience and generating and testing actions in the real world (such as our civilization is). When we do put the burden of proof on an opposing presumption to our own, we do not (necessarily need to) do it on the basis of best evidence. Rather, we choose our presumption as a policy, and then continue action whether or not we ever test that policy against evidence.

Our ignorance is our reality, and presumption (and arguments from ignorance) is how we cope with our reality while pursuing our goals that are only subjectively important. Yes, only subjectively important. Priorities and values are not universally important. Don't judge the utility of inference products in contexts of an individual while neglecting their own knowledge, memory, imagination and attention, and in particular, don't judge the rationality of an individual by their inference products.

We do not suffer from self-deception. Overconfidence and self-deception are not genuine phenomena. We commonly lie, for social reasons, and those lies can run deep, but in the end, lies are all they are. We can act as if something is true for our own reasons, a bit different than deception because it is only presumption and then, sometimes, testing that presumption. After all, we genuinely are forever ignorant of the truth. Acting as if, or, put differently, generating actions and testing them in the real world, is all we really have as an option.

That's the core of what my epistemology motivates, minus a few key details and some logic examples and discussion.

item.title: Levent is my favorite gender role
item.description:
Last Friday, this guy I once did a pie-eating challenge with proved the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with a little help from Claude. 

He released his announcement as a spoken word poem:

It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. 

Everyone in the world is trying to make this historic moment about themselves and their hobbyhorse. This essay is my attempt.

To start off, let’s take a look at Fernando Borretti’s analysis, which tries to match Levent’s energy:

The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on. 

This is a truly epic misreading. Levent’s memo is no suicide note; it’s a garden-variety case of terminal Chuunibyou.

What is Chuunibyou?

The Japanese term chuunibyou (Chinese: 中二病), literally “middle-school second-year syndrome,” refers to adolescents who act melodramatic, adopt grandiose personas, or convince themselves they possess secret knowledge or supernatural powers. 

For Westerners: a chuunibyou, or chuuni for short, is somewhere in the convex hull of weeaboo, mad lad, and romantic. The archetypal chuuni is this generational mad lad.

Another classic chuuni is the OP of the reddit story My girlfriend doesn't want me to hang Andúril on the wall:

So last weekend I let myself go to a convention and I bought The Sword of the Heir of Isildur. I even bought it for an absolute bargain. When I got home with it, my girlfriend got mad and said she didn't want to hang it anywhere in the house.

My headcanon for how that conversation went down: 

"Hey babe, guess what I just bought for an absolute bargain?"
"What?"
Unsheathes. "Andúril, Flame of the West—"
"No way am I—"
Sweep. "First known as Narsil, forged in the First Age by Telchar of Nogrod—"
"—displaying that monstrosity—"
Riposte. "Wielded by Elendil, last Lord of Andúnië—"
"—in my living—"
Spin, knocking over potted orchids, grandiose flourish. "Reforged from its broken shards by Aragorn son of Arathorn, the Elessar, true heir to the throne of Gondor!!"
"—room!!!"

I was recently sniped by a Chinese aphorism:

人终被年少而不可得之物捆其一身
In the end, all are trapped by that which we longed for in youth and could never have.

This is a chuuni quine. It carries the melodramatic structure of chuuni thinking, and is secretly self-referential. In the end, all are trapped by that which we longed for in youth and could never have: chuunibyou.

In the West, chuunibyou manifests covertly in YA fantasy, typified by the great works of J. R. R. Tolkien and Ursula Le Guin. But primarily, it is an object of shame: no man has done more damage to the Western psyche than Miguel de Cervantes, who single-handedly poisoned our infinite well of child-like exuberance with his sneerclub magnum opus Don Quixote. That’s why all Westerners must turn, in the end, to the East to find their share of unabashed chuunibyou content. 

Both men and women can be chuuni – my wife Jasmine is a 5-dan Go player who introduced me to anime. Other than Jasmine, Ursula Le Guin is my favorite chuuni lady, and the culture is full of depictions of chuuni girls, such as Fischl from Genshin Impact. 

If you’re already reaching your cringe tolerance, buckle up. The middle of this essay is written in the unreliable narration of my inner chuunibyou. Here’s another Chinese aphorism to help you through it:

我不尴尬，尴尬的就是别人
As long as I don’t cringe, the cringe becomes other people’s problem.

Repeat this mantra every seven seconds.

There are only two gender roles

There’s an unsourced quote in the depths of my memory (maybe from Duncan Sabien?): “What people don’t understand is that there are actually two male gender roles: boy and man.” Here’s my gender-neutral generalization:

What people don’t understand is that there are only two gender roles: Chuuni and Suit.

Chuuni is romantic, ephemeral, tragic, irresponsible, and grandiose. Suit is stoic, inexorable, procedural, responsible, and pragmatic. These roles are primarily aesthetic preferences, and lie askew to values or competence. 

To train your chuuni-suit classifier, let’s play a game. What’s Chuuni and what’s Suit?

Marx: The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains.

Chuuni.

Hegel: The state, which is the realized substantive will, having its reality in the particular self-consciousness raised to the plane of the universal, is absolutely rational. This substantive unity is its own motive and absolute end. In this end freedom attains its highest right. This end has the highest right over the individual, whose highest duty in turn is to be a member of the state.

Suit.

Kierkegaard: In one of the tales of the Romantic School which evinces the greatest genius, there is one character who has no desire to write poetry like the others among whom he lives, because it is a waste of time and deprives him of the true enjoyment; he prefers to live.

Chuuni. Replace “poetry” with “math papers” and arrive at a faithful representation of Levent.

David Hilbert’s tombstone: "We must know / We shall know."

Peak chuuni mad lad.

Terry Tao: Then you can do factory production–type, industrial-scale mathematics, which doesn't really exist right now.

Suit.

Chuunis inevitably appear in every space. There are chuuni mathematicians, like Euler, Hilbert, Grothendieck, and Erdős. There are literary chuunis, like Le Guin and Tolkien.

Rationalist chuunis abound.

Never confess to me that you are just as flawed as I am unless you can tell me what you plan to do about it. Afterward you will still have plenty of flaws left, but that’s not the point; the important thing is to do better, to keep moving ahead, to take one more step forward. Tsuyoku naritai!
~ Eliezer Yudkowsky, Tsuyoku naritai! (I want to become stronger)

There are even evil tech oligarch chuunis like Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk.

As for Suit, I’ll define it only by recalling the phrase “the suit wears the man.” An interesting paradox is that most artists are naturally chuuni, so the stand-out characters playing “Suits” (e.g. Don Draper, Harvey Specter, Barney Stinson, and The Wolf of Wall Street) are actually distorted chuuni LARPs of Suits. Chain-smoking myself to death in my Manhattan corner office while juggling sexual escapades is a slight romanticization of corporate middle management.

We don’t get to see the real Suits in the media, because the real corpos are boring as fuck. They’re stuck in the third war room of the week root-causing the PR that impacted the availability of Outlook.

The Romantic Moment

Central to the chuuni spirit is the total rejection of practicality in pursuit of the romantic moment. A Tesla Roadster that makes one successful somersault deserves celebration even if it costs six figures and a twenty-year waitlist, and even if it comes down in a flaming inferno. Cool guys don’t look at explosions anyway. 

The yearning for that single poignant moment catches rockets, starts revolutions, and fuels options markets. Here’s Le Guin pointing to the romantic moment in Malafrena (read carefully):

A liberal is one for whom the means justify the ends.

One epic last dance justifies itself, irrespective of outcomes.

A level above mine

Mathematicians are a fairly chuunibyou lot, and I am a very chuunibyou mathematician. At work, I am Professor Xiaoyu He, Stanford PhD. But I have a second identity, alkjash, a username I button-mashed in grade school and decided was my true name after reading The Earthsea Cycle. You might think having a suit identity and a chuuni identity makes me less pure as a chuuni. You would be wrong. Having a secret chuuni identity is at least as chuuni as commuting to work by Naruto run.

In terms of chuunibyou, Levent Alpöge operates on a level above mine. When we studied together at the Duluth REU, he had already earned a reputation as a lovable freak of nature. 

At the time, eating competitions were a staple of Duluth REU culture, and Levent was in a league of his own. The Pig’s Trough challenge at Betty’s Pies consists of a full plate of pie and ice cream; I remember slogging through the challenge in around twenty minutes and literally shaking with hyperglycemia for an hour after. Levent wolfed the Pig’s Trough down in four minutes flat, a record that stands to this day. [Edit: I've been informed that Levent's record was broken by Colin Defant.]

He was the only person to finish the Eiffel Tower burger challenge, with six cheesy patties and a full plate of fries. The two camp counselors who tried this challenge both ended the day puking their guts out in the bathroom. Levent went home and ran a 10K right after.

While the rest of us plodded along and solved research problems with Olympiad tricks, Levent went ahead and learned the Hardy-Littlewood circle method, a monstrosity that should have taken at least a semester to master. I could keep up with Levent in a fifteen-minute conversation, but he seemed able to zoom off and keep working indefinitely, without apparent fatigue or satiety.

By the time I graduated college, of the hundreds of top math students I knew (half of them IMO gold medalists), perhaps five were like Levent: Alex Honnold-type anomalies of psychology who could keep up a sprinter's pace in a mathematical marathon. Akhil Mathew, who patiently failed to explain spectral sequences to me over and over, was another. At that time, I was too awe-struck to see them fully as human beings; I wonder now if Levent and Akhil had a hard time relating to us mortals.

In August, my AI doompost caught Levent’s attention, and we reconnected over text about AI, math, and x-risk. That’s when I pegged him for a fellow chuuni:

alkjash: Just talked to Hugo Duminil-Copin who told me to slap you for him (for announcing Jacobian so disrespectfully)

Levent: he is right btw [...] Wait, could i have Hugo’s number? he could curse me out directly. 

If you do not understand chuuni, then it might appear to you that Levent experienced character growth here. But this is all perfectly explicable in the aesthetic logic of romantic moments. 

Disproving the Jacobian conjecture via tweet is a romantic moment, and being cursed out for it by a Fields Medalist is an equally romantic moment. 

The battle for Navier-Stokes between OpenAI’s professionalized math team and Levent and Tristan Buckmaster’s “hobby project” is the archetypal battle between Suit and Chuuni. Being personally bullied by OpenAI is a romantic moment, as is taking a stand against The Man for your bromance.

Proving GRH just after Tao declares the “end of math’s romantic hero era” is a romantic moment of epic proportions, as is making a farce of it by joking about the length of the proof.

The history of all hitherto existing AI safety discourse is the history of gender struggle

Like most of my essays these days, this essay is not really about Levent, or about me. It’s about AI safety. 

What better way to convince yourself you possess secret knowledge or supernatural powers than by working with internal models at a frontier AI lab? The recent DeepMind documentary The Thinking Game is chock full of romantic moments in the life of Demis Hassabis, from his heartbreaking defeat in a chess tournament to the solution of the protein folding problem. Is it any wonder that all the Levents of the world are flocking to AI?

As Serret tempts Sparrowhawk in A Wizard of Earthsea, so too AI companies tempt even the altruistic chuunis who want to save the world:

Serret: Only shadow can fight shadow. Only darkness can defeat the dark. Listen, Sparrowhawk!
[...]
Shaken and tormented, he did not answer. She held his hand now in both of hers, looking into his face. The sun had fallen into the mists that dulled the horizon, and the air too had grown dull, but her face grew bright with praise and triumph as she watched him and saw his will shaken within him. Softly she whispered, “You will be mightier than all men, a king among men. You will rule, and I will rule with you –” 
[...]
Sparrowhawk looked down at Serret. “It is light that defeats the dark,” he said stammering, – “Light.” 

Our saving grace, I hope, is that there will always be more light chuunis than dark chuunis, and the bat signal of AI safety is even more magnetic than the siren song of AI capabilities. The Suits invoke the inevitability of incentives, and believe that AI progress cannot be stopped because billions of dollars. But here’s what the Suits always miss: 

What’s more romantic than making a billion dollars? Walking away from a billion dollars.

That is not to say that AI safety is all chuunibyou; indeed, we are ourselves deeply split along the chuuni-suit axis. In 2023, Vanessa Kosoy wrote of the great Christiano-Yudkowsky takeoff speed debate:

In the existential AI safety community, there is an ongoing debate between positions situated differently on some axis which doesn't have a common agreed-upon name, but where Christiano and Yudkowsky can be regarded as representatives of the two directions[1]. For the sake of this review, I will dub the camps gravitating to the different ends of this axis "Prosers" (after prosaic alignment) and "Poets"[2]. Christiano is a Proser, and so are most people in AI safety groups in the industry. Yudkowsky is a typical Poet [sort-of Poet, but there's an important departure from my characterization below], people in MIRI and the agent foundations community tend to also be such.

I propose that the true name of Proser is Suit. Here’s a passage indicative of Christiano’s tenor on AI takeoff:

Humanity usually solves technical problems by iterating and fixing failures; we often resolve tough methodological disagreements very slowly by seeing what actually works and having our failures thrown in our face. But it will probably be possible to build valuable AI products without solving alignment, and so reality won’t “force us” to solve alignment until it’s too late. This seems like a case where we will have to be unusually reliant on careful reasoning rather than empirical feedback loops for some of the highest-level questions.

I propose that the true name of Poet is Chuunibyou. Here’s a passage from Yudkowsky’s list of lethalities:

The nanomachinery builds diamondoid bacteria, that replicate with solar power and atmospheric CHON, maybe aggregate into some miniature rockets or jets so they can ride the jetstream to spread across the Earth's atmosphere, get into human bloodstreams and hide, strike on a timer.  Losing a conflict with a high-powered cognitive system looks at least as deadly as "everybody on the face of the Earth suddenly falls over dead within the same second".

I propose that the split of AI safety into two camps should be understood not as an epistemic battle but as an aesthetic one: Suit against Chuuni. METR reports speak to the Suit, and FOOM stories speak to the Chuuni. 

As the dust settles, the fracture between the cluster around Yudkowsky and LessWrong and the cluster around Christiano and ARC seems to have only solidified. Here is LessWrong messaging:

And here’s ARC messaging (from the NYT’s Looking for the Formula to Stop an Apocalypse):

[Mike Winer] calculated about a 50 percent chance that humans would lose control of powerful A.I. systems in the next five years; 22 percent that most people would eventually die as a result; 1 percent that ARC would help prevent catastrophe by using math to look inside an A.I. model and estimate the possibility of a rare disaster that no amount of testing would catch.

“That might not sound like good odds,” he told the visiting mathematicians. “But a 1 percent chance of saving humanity is probably a lot more important than anything else you could be doing.”

Will this gender war divide us forever? I see hope for a true synthesis of both aesthetics in the new generation of AI safety leaders.

For another example, take Jacob Tsimerman, founder and director of the Mathematical AI Safety Institute at Berkeley, the new face of mathematical AI safety, and somehow Levent’s undergrad advisor. Jacob, like Nate, integrates Chuuni and Suit in one person. 

Jacob had his world-class romantic moment by announcing his pivot to AI safety on the same day he won the Fields Medal. Initially, he announced that he would go to OpenAI, then backed out and made off with $10 million of OpenAI compute credits without spending a day at the job. He also turned out to be some kind of organizational savant, putting together within months a cracked team and a permanent institute at Berkeley that may host up to a hundred senior mathematicians by next fall. 

Imagine how much syncing with stakeholders it took to pull that off.

Synthesis

Much of my job as a math professor is helping students bridge the abyss between their youthful flights of fancy and the responsibilities of adulthood. Our seminar rooms overflow with young men and women ready to lay down a lifetime of toil in service of that one romantic moment, that one Andrew Wiles or Yitang Zhang final reveal, but few of them have the stomach for the committee meetings and exam grading that will surely intervene. Masullo is but one face in this crowd. We live in a cursed world where these students must grow up quickly, more quickly than nature prepared them for, and yet I cannot help but see forcing adulthood down their throats as a crime against their inner Levents. 

What the haters don’t understand is that Levent was always right about reality. We do not live in a world of atoms or a world of bits; we live in a world of romantic moments. One time during grad school, I took the BART up to Berkeley to meet Zvi Mowshowitz, and he spent twenty minutes on the sidewalk extolling the virtues of a particular Dungeons and Dragons worldbuilding guide, which describes a world in which magical humans walk among us surrounded by probability-bending forcefields. The kind of forcefield that starts a philosophical movement through a Harry Potter fanfic, or gets Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO. 

Zvi’s story was one of many that taught me to cherish my inner Levent. Cauterizing chuunibyou, burying it under a mountain of shame and responsibility, is not maturity; it is blinding yourself to the drama and romance of life. Integration is maturity. 

Nate Soares and Jacob Tsimerman point the way forward: to the end of our collective gender role confusion, and to a synthesis of Chuuni and Suit. We need to grow up, but we should never abandon Levent.

item.title: Open Weight Models are not the immediate problem
item.description:
Disclaimer: I work at a company that serves open weight models.

The biggest current problem humans face from AI is recursive self improvement, leading to more and more powerful AIs, until an AI is so powerful and intelligent that it cannot be contained (if its creators are even trying) and then it will reshape the world as it sees fit.[1]

The immediate necessary solution is stopping frontier AI development. This is a very specific ask.[2] It does not require banning open weight models, or banning AI, or banning data-centers, or a number of other related (sometimes useful, not necessary, maybe counterproductive) things.

Current open weight models are not about to start recursively self improving. They’re not intelligent or long-running enough to do this. Furthermore, non-frontier labs will not be able to use them to do RSI because training and R&D require tons of compute. Frontier internal AIs are far ahead of open weights models in terms of AI R&D and general 'intelligence' and that gap is probably widening. [3]


The solution: external regulation

The companies will not self-regulate. Someone with a big stick needs to threaten them. There is a bill in congress, the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, to pause advanced AI development. There's been some previous discussion of this: In general the bill seems directionally correct. I'm afraid it won't go through the federal government, and if it does it may be too slow.

If you live in California, it seems the best thing you can do is ask your representatives to implement an immediate pause on frontier AI development, as this could be faster and seems more likely to go through than the bill.

If you live in another state, telling your representatives to support the Act seems to be the best thing you can do.

This and telling people seems to be the best thing I know of. [4]


Mixed messaging is confusing

  1. I was at a town hall last week by my representative, Ro Khanna. I asked him a leading question about AI safety and pausing frontier AI development. His response was to discuss GLM-5.3 being dangerous for hackers, and mention takeover as an afterthought.[5]

This was worse than I expected. Khanna has expressed some level of support for the Ban Superintelligence Act. I set him up for a very obvious answer. What I would’ve liked to hear is “Yes, we need to slowdown frontier AI development now”, instead of over-indexing on misuse.

  1. I’ve noticed on Reddit and Twitter that people react negatively to calls for regulation. They see it as a way for Anthropic to take over. I empathize with this because Anthropic behaves in power seeking ways[6] and has made calls for regulation.

The obvious solution to thwart the above criticism is to say “No, we specifically need to stop/pause frontier AI development. This will not give Anthropic an edge”. It helps to be able to say this if the messaging is generally consistent. [7]

  1. I've seen discussions of risk from current AIs, such as long-running rogue AIs. These sound dangerous but are a non-sequitur for x-risk. Prosaic risks are solvable given time and effort poured into improving cybersecurity and biosecurity and other -securities. The reason this is not happening now is because the labs are putting the majority of their resources into racing towards ASI, both shrinking the time to new models and taking away compute that could be used for making the world resilient.


Okay, cool, but why not just ban open weights models at the same time?

There are a number of reasons for this. In approximate order of importance:

  1. There’s not actually a good case for this, and trying to make a good case for this weakens the actual case, that is RSI and ASI. Same problem with leaving out existential risk when lobbying: you get policies that don’t do what you want because they don’t understand/haven’t been convinced of the actual problem.
  2. (1) but for the average persons[8] perception. The general opinion of Anthropic seems to be that they’re doing all the doom stuff for money. This is understandable from the outside because Anthropic is constantly contradicting themselves.[9] People, when they see a push for regulation that Anthropic has spoken in favor of, assume it will benefit Anthropic and reduce competition.
  3. I think that open weights models, kept to some level (below the frontier but also below certain capability levels, these levels being determined by how hardened the world is) are good for preventing concentration of power and maintaining democracy.

These same arguments apply to banning all AI, or banning AI because it’s misleading, or any other regulation that fails to directly interact with the actual problem, that is RSI leading to ASI.


Conclusion

If frontier AI development gets paused and open weight models also get banned then I’d be disappointed but happy overall. [10][11]

I worry that the ask is getting diluted and this leads to policy not doing the urgent thing. It would be nice for the majority of (AI safety) people to be on the same page about what that urgent thing is (preventing RSI leading to uncontrollable ASI).

I think there are a lot of tech-adjacent people who would be more on board with this if it was clear that this is specifically about pausing/slowing down frontier AI development. [12]

  1. ^

    This is bad. There are many failure points along the way, it's irreversible, RSI means more speed and less human understanding at each stage.. Also you might just not like the idea of uncontrollable AI.

  2. ^

    There are things to do after this, like enforce this for everyone (including our favorite player China). I won’t harp on this as AI-2040 goes into better detail. I tried writing out my ideal scenario and it was similar to Plan A: international regulation, slow down the frontier, disperse AI benefits.

  3. ^

    Open weight models are pretty good at cyber, but this is solvable: invest in cybersecurity, and hardening the world. This has the added benefit of making the world better.

  4. ^

    I live in California, and I used ControlAI to send a message to my representatives. I changed the message they filled it out with slightly to emphasize that California should take action now, independent of the Act, but kept the recommendation to meet with ControlAI. ControlAI consulted on the Ban Superintelligence Act.

  5. ^

    I was worried his GLM-5.3 comment was anti-open weight models, but given this article his views seem good: He wants CISA to put more effort into cybersecurity.

  6. ^

    That is, Anthropic the corporation is well-modeled as trying to amass power, ostensibly for instrumental purposes like having enough compute to scale to ASI.

  7. ^

    Wanting to argue about this with people is a large reason I wrote this post. I was trying to convince a friend that regulation was good, and their immediate take was that Anthropic was aiming for regulatory capture, and I said no that's not the goal - but I don't set the goal on my own, it's some amalgamation of what everyone wants.

  8. ^

    It's probably more accurate to say 'average tech-adjacent' person, as I'm basing this on Reddit/Twitter. But I've also noticed this with people who don't know anything about tech.

  9. ^

    There’s been a lot of discussion on Anthropic's failings recently.

  10. ^

    At least in the short term.. Longer term I’m worried that this is the path to consolidation of power/ disempowerment. Disempowerment is de facto bad imo, but also instrumentally bad if it happens too soon, so that it reduces the governments ability to regulate AI (e.g in AI-2040 almost all of the good things for the average person come out of regulation and democracy).

  11. ^

    Frontier AI development getting paused and open weight models also getting paused at current levels seems reasonable.

  12. ^

    Instead, on twitter you're fighting against: Guy who likes coding with AI, Evil Accelerationist, Liberal Democracy Enjoyer.

item.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated As Nvidia CEO at Behest of President Trump
item.description:
In the evening of November 22, Donald Trump said he ‘hoped’ the Nvidia board would rehire Jensen Huang, as the ‘best thing for the Company.’

Shortly after that Donald Trump called the Nvidia board. On the morning of November 23, Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia.

Andrew Curran: President Trump live on CNBC [on Monday night]: ‘I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly.’

It was an excellent day for the stock market. Over three trillion dollars in value was added. Nvidia alone was up over 30% on the day.

It was a tragic day in many other ways. This may go down as one of the greatest scandals in history. It was a dark day for our democracy and free market economy and the rule of law, and for the integrity of our government. This will forever, or at least for the next two years, factor into every decision made, and every trade in the stock market. It was the triumph of hostile action, of deliberately setting things up to collapse without you.

In the era of Donald Trump, it was the ultimate ‘nothing matters’ moment. It likely means that Nvidia is going to go back to maximizing, in an adversarial way, how many chips it can sell to China, and to those who will smuggle into China.

It also means that, as in the playbook of OpenAI’s Battle of the Board, the tech vibe army and its commanders are hard at work gloating, and trying to pillage, and to memory hole all of the things Jensen Huang did. They celebrate, emboldened now more than ever to play a hostile game where they make themselves impossible to fire by threatening to blow up their companies, including by threatening the scalps of anyone who dares oppose them.

They are acting as if this was a hit job from The New York Times, rather than pointing out true and important facts about the world that others were also scrambling to report. They are calling that reporting a ‘failure’ because Jensen Huang is once again CEO of Nvidia. There are continued attempts to blame some cabal.

These people work on vibes, so they think that because they ‘won’ they should therefore get rewarded in various ways. They will try to imply this means there shouldn’t be tightening or enforcement of export controls, and other such things. I hope and expect Congress to think otherwise, all the more so.

This is far from over. The national security state is no doubt furious. There are going to be extensive Congressional investigations, and also extensive criminal investigations. Jensen Huang is scheduled for three House committees already. The reporting will continue. There is new reporting on many fronts.

Table of Contents

  1. I Got This One Wrong.
  2. How Did It Happen?
  3. Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia.
  4. The Trump Put.
  5. The Whole Affairs.
  6. Better to Be Feared Than Loved.
  7. The Law of No Evidence.
  8. The War Against the Press.
  9. There’s Going to Be an Investigation.
  10. More on Chip Smuggling.
  11. The Market Roars.
  12. Morals Shmorals.
  13. The Lighter Side.

I Got This One Wrong

To state the obvious, I said this was not going to happen. I was wrong. One of the goals of this post is to explain my understanding, now, of why I was wrong. There were multiple things I got wrong. Most importantly, I did not understand how much Jensen Huang had set everything up to collapse like a house of cards without him. I did not expect the stock market to drop so far that a full Trump Put would be in play, where he would be willing to accept all the consequences of this action. I also expected the national security concerns to be more of a showstopper than they were.

Others got this wrong too, or at least put this as unlikely, although I got it more wrong. Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday and then soared 31% on the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, which shows they did not expect it.

What I continue to believe I was not wrong about was the essential actions of Jensen Huang, and that it is not acceptable for him to continue as CEO of Nvidia. This is a clear and present danger to national security. It is happening anyway, because, in a way I did not anticipate, not having Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia may be an even bigger danger.

How Did It Happen?

This was the Nvidia board announcement of Jensen Huang’s return.

Nvidia Newsroom:

NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

Ryan Gould, Ian King, and Edward Ludlow (Bloomberg): “Thank you all for the second chance,” he said. “I am gonna be a better CEO the second time around.”

For now Jensen Huang is being magnanimous, being thankful for the second chance and saying he was going to do better, and apologizing and saying he is going to therapy. We will see if that lasts.

The board did not consult management, including the interim CEO. They got a call from Donald Trump, and then did what they had to do.

The explanation is that now that they are satisfied that Jensen Huang being reinstated ‘poses no national security risk.’ As literally presented this is Obvious Nonsense. Of course Jensen Huang leading Nvidia poses a national security risk. What they mean is that Trump told them to do it anyway, that they would not be held responsible for that, and that not reinstating him would present both a national security risk and also a personal job security risk.

The Editorial Board (WSJ): Mr. Trump claimed his Administration had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Nvidia, and Mr. Huang was “exonerated.” That must be the quickest very thorough investigation in history. All of this suggests Mr. Trump assured the board that his Administration wouldn’t punish the company for possible violations of export controls or securities laws if they rehired the CEO.

Later in the post I will examine exactly how much pressure was involved here.

Donald Trump Intervened Personally to Install Jensen Huang at Nvidia

At a high level, this is the story of The Fall and Rise of Jensen Huang. None of these facts is meaningfully in dispute:

  1. Jensen Huang and Nvidia sold a lot of chips to China, and sold a lot of chips to what are now known to be chip smuggling operations, and engaged in a systematic adversarial lobbying and technical compliance campaign while Jensen has a lot of affairs including with both a direct report and also one of the larger chip smugglers who is also an alleged spy according to government reports that know of the affair.
  2. The New York Times reports this information in public.
  3. Jensen Huang, under pressure and about to be fired, resigns from Nvidia.
  4. Nvidia stock tanks. Other stocks tank.
  5. Donald Trump personally calls for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. He ‘speaks to the board directly and indirectly’ on this matter. He makes it clear what he wants, and that he does not consider Jensen Huang a national security risk.
  6. The Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang, in a surprise move, without consulting management.

It is very clear that step #4 was the key in causing step #5. Trump has said as much.

I did not sufficiently seriously consider the possibility of #4 happening to this large an extent, or that it would be sufficient to trigger this style of intervention, and I predicted the national security state and others would fight back against it harder than they did.

Aleph (November 18): The Jensen Huang affair is the first time I’ve ever seen NYC finance types be more clearpilled about a situation than tech people, which is interesting

Samuel Hammond (November 19): Realism vs sycophancy.

It was exactly the NYC finance types, rather than the San Francisco types or tech types, that made this happen, and that place such a high value on Jensen Huang, and that forced the President’s hand.

The Trump Put

Nvidia was judged, in this sense, Too Big to Fail (to have Jensen Huang as CEO).

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ):

The artificial-intelligence boom that had powered the U.S. stock market and economy for months was coming undone. Jensen Huang, the longtime CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia had been ousted following revelations of two affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Investors were hitting sell on the entire AI trade.

President Trump told associates there was only one solution: getting Huang, a friend and ally, his job back.

… What followed were a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the vice president and other top administration officials relayed [Attorney General Todd] Blanche’s assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a leader Trump hadn’t even heard of when he began his second term.

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ): He said he was told the government hadn’t found Huang had done anything illegal, only that “he made some indiscretions having to do with other things.” Trump said once he heard there was no illegal activity on Huang’s part, “I began a push.”

Charles Gasparino: BREAKING: Major investors were alerting people close to the White House after last week’s AI-stock debacle that the probability was near 100% that the country was heading for a recession, given the unwind of the AI trade and how it would impact spending across the tech ecosystem.

It’s seen as the major reason why @SecScottBessent suddenly joined his boss in calling for @JensenHuang to be reinstated because it would at least temporarily pause the market convulsion, my sources (who have been pretty good on this) tell me.

… Now my opinion: There may be a short term gain, but the potential for long term pain is pretty high. Huang coming back doesn’t mean he can come back to do biz as usual. How will he sell to China? The investigations from Congress are coming. How will @SecScottBessent and @SecRubio (much less @howardlutnick ) rationalize what we will be discovering about chips going to China?

Jay Shooster: Jensen’s reinstatement should give you an idea of how short-term economic incentives may prevent us from simply shutting down AI models even when they pose glaring dangers to our national security.

Jensen Huang denies that this was ‘solely at the president’s request.’

Jon Swartz (Techstrong.ai): While Huang acknowledged that the Trump administration provided assurances to the board that his return would not pose a national security risk, he called claims that he was brought back solely at the president’s request “completely untrue.” Instead, Huang said the board made its decision after it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts.”

This is a clear case of Exact Words. Yes, of course the board ‘evaluated the entire situation’ and ‘gathered facts’ in addition to the fact that Trump very strongly wanted him reinstated, and what he was doing to make that happen. And yes, those additional facts mattered, especially the stock drop, and they would have pushed back harder if circumstances were different. He was not the ‘sole’ cause.

This is also a clear case of ‘who are you kidding.’ Trump says his intervention was ‘very important.’ He says that the board did what ‘we’ wanted and that he was ‘represented’ at the board meeting. Previously, the board had said, according to Faber, ‘no effing way’ Huang was coming back.

The President did it.

The President personally picking the CEO of one of the world’s largest companies is not typically the kind of thing a free market Democracy with robust rule of law goes around doing.

Tad DeHaven (Cato Institute): The President Has No Business Picking Nvidia’s CEO… Why was that the president’s deal to make?

Greg Ip: The Nvidia scandal is the logical result of America’s slide into state capitalism under Trump. The backlash may mark a turning point, back to the separation of board room and state.

Scott Lincicome: Yes it is. And I hope Greg is right.

Greg Ip (WSJ): Trump’s break with precedent (he led a similar trip in his first term) symbolizes how government and corporate interests have become more tightly intertwined in his presidency. Nvidia’s controversial sale of chips to China, if not Huang’s indiscretions, were the logical outcome.

… Shortly after returning to office, Trump reeled back enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act which bars American companies from bribing foreign officials to win business. Overzealous enforcement “actively harms American economic competitiveness and, therefore, national security,” he wrote.

He approved sales of sensitive technology, such as F-35 jet fighters to Saudi Arabia and Nvidia chips to the United Arab Emirates, despite some U.S. officials’ fears the tech would leak to China.

He also began meddling directly in company business, including taking direct stakes in companies such as Intel, critical minerals producers and the missile business of L3Harris.

… Imagine, [Robert Lighthizer] said, that an adviser to Ronald Reagan had used Huang’s “addiction” logic in the 1980s and suggested selling American space-based missile-defense tech to the Soviets “because then they’ll get addicted to us. The whole notion is beyond preposterous.”

Editorial Board (WaPo): Maybe Nvidia’s board made the right call, but this is not how free markets are supposed to work.

… Trump acknowledged that the recent market correction “probably” influenced his intervention, though he said “the bigger impact was the long term.” A president worried about falling stock prices shouldn’t respond by rearranging the management team of one of America’s most valuable companies.

… Huang’s extraordinary resurrection will inevitably teach Silicon Valley something about power. The wrong lesson would be that executives need more intertwined relationships with Washington. Healthy capitalism depends on companies succeeding because they satisfy customers and investors, not because their executives curry the president’s favor. Huang might be indispensable, but that’s for Nvidia to decide.

Why would it be the wrong lesson to think that you need to cozy up to power, if power has decided that it can replace or reinstate you? That sounds like the right lesson. If you don’t want them to draw that conclusion, how about making it not true?

How bad is this intervention, on the scale of ‘that was Tuesday in the Trump Administration’ to ‘Nvidia is now kind of nationalized.’

Greg Ip: Nvidia is becoming a government sponsored enterprise (GSE). Like the original GSEs, Fannie & Freddie, the state guides its mission and governance; and its success now depends as much on state favor as business prowess.

PoliMath: This is a consequence of the fact that SCOTUS let the Biden admin get away with pressuring tech companies to censor social media during Covid. They set the precedent that “the state guides (the company) mission and governance and success depends on state favor”

I said that was a bad idea at the time! Oh well, too bad I lost that argument. It sure sucks to have no consequences for awful behavior, doesn’t it?

All sufficiently large companies, and definitely all such AI companies, depend on not incurring the wrath of the Federal Government or the White House.

The Whole Affairs

Yashar Ali: NEW: The Wall Street Journal reports that Jensen Huang disclosed additional affairs to Nvidia’s board on Sunday.

Amrith Ramkumar, Josh Dawsey, C. Ryan Barber and Robbie Whelan (WSJ): Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.

Misha: The implication from this picture is one of the affairs is with trump

Lain on the Blockchain: Dwarkesh is a very obvious and archetypal example of a federal agent btw.

Dwarkesh Patel: that’s why I also slept with jensen.

That’s additional affairs, plural, so that means a minimum of four.

Better to Be Feared Than Loved

When Sam Altman returned to OpenAI, he purged those who had opposed him.

As Jensen Huang returns to Nvidia, one assumes he will attempt to do the same, to the extent that he sees such folks that way, or needs to send a message.

I do not see the Nvidia board as in the same position as the OpenAI board.

The OpenAI board fired Altman for reasons it could not explain, out of the blue, in a decision it was not forced to make. If I was Altman, I too would have replaced the board as a condition of my return. It is unsurprising that he also purged those who sided too strongly with the board.

Jim Cramer wants to know why the Chairman and all who voted against Huang don’t resign. This is why: The Nvidia board had no meaningful choice. They tried their best to keep him on board pending a nominal investigation for as long as possible. They asked Jensen to resign based on highly public information. Jensen Huang could choose not to overhaul his board. Donald Trump explicitly praised the board as doing a great job.

My expectation is that he will overhaul the board anyway.

Why? Because, whether or not he is loved, Jensen Huang reigns largely in fear.

Reigning in fear is a valid way to reign. Many tech icons, such as Steve Jobs, reigned in fear and did great things. Machiavelli approves.

The board was unanimous in reinstating Jensen Huang. One guess what would have happened to anyone who voted no. Donald Trump is calling Jensen Huang ‘a Great Patriot and a National Treasure.’ Anyone seen The Death of Stalin? Rings some bells.

Rather than owning this basic fact, certain people gaslight us by showing us that, why, everyone cheers so loudly for Comrade Jensen Huang, no one stops clapping, they must truly love Jensen Huang and they definitely don’t fear him or want to be caught as the one not clapping. Nor are they clapping because their company stock was down 40% and is now up 30% from there.

This here sounds like an employee with a perfectly normal loving attitude who definitely is not trying to flatter anyone, oh no, definitely not.

What about the article David Sacks was photographing?

Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle (NYTimes): As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

My biggest complaint here is that these aren’t very original. gotta ding him for style points here.

Derek Thompson: Jensen Huang being a Jesse Armstrong character has been a fun revelation.

… “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish.

… Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career.

… Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

Sounds like many visionary and highly successful tech founders. You may not like it, indeed I hope you do not like it, but there is a plausible case that this is what peak performance looks like.

I know how easy it is for an article like this to blow things out of proportion, and to find selective facts and string them together to paint a picture. I do not think that is happening here. I think that Jensen Huang was the person being described here.

The Law of No Evidence

Donald Trump’s congratulatory message clears Jensen Huang by saying that there is ‘no reason to believe’ that Jensen Huang’s return poses a national security risk, and that it ‘does not possess evidence’ that Huang ‘acted unlawfully.’

Donald Trump: The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.

The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.

Remember the Law of No Evidence. Any claim that there is “no evidence” of something is evidence of bullshit. This is an even more clear case than usual, in that there is very obviously quite a lot of evidence that his return poses a national security risk.

Even if we know everything Jensen Huang did, and even if Alice Huang turns out to have only been a chip smuggler at large for profit rather than a spy, Jensen Huang engaged in a systematic campaign to sell chips to China, and have chips smuggled into China, and to compromise the United States government on this, while taking a fully adversarial stance. He may or may not have technically broken related laws along the way, at least in any way you could prove.

How much of not a national security risk is Jensen Huang? This much, very safe.

Weijia Jiang: In an ongoing interview, Trump says if Huang had not been reinstated at Nvidia, Xi might have called and asked him to lead a Chinese company. If Huang was “mad” enough at the U.S. Trump said he may have done it… adding he has some of their “blood in him.”

The New York Times reported on one of the biggest financial news stories of all time, and one of the biggest scandals in American history, and a clear threat to national security, repeatedly for days on end.

The response was to declare war against The New York Times, and assume this must be some grand conspiracy, and also to declare some sort of ‘victory’ against it.

Toby Rogers: The @NYTimes ‘ coordinated assault on Jensen Huang is astonishing. Three to five hit pieces a day. Front page. Thinly sourced. Every day for two weeks. If the NY Times spent even 1% of that energy going after Epstein’s clients or Big Pharma, the world would be a better place.

Jensen Huang and Elon Musk are the wrong type of rich and the @NYTimes hates that.

bone: asking my agent swarm to do oppo research on every journalist at the NYT, examining their sex lives, interviewing their ex girlfriends, investigating their marriages, their personal debts, their financial connections to Anthropic and EA causes.

we are the media now.

I have not seen any evidence of a coordinated campaign. If there is one, I am not involved in any way.

When I heard about ‘the Nvidia smear campaign’ and that someone’s heart went out to those put at risk, I initially thought ‘oh that’s nice that Olivia Moore worried about all the victims of Nvidia’s smear campaigns.’ I knew some people. Then I quickly realized, no, she meant a supposed smear campaign against Nvidia.

I know the feeling of trying to build generational wealth while someone else is trying to win a Pulitzer. Incredibly disheartening.

I know the feeling of trying to do accountability journalism in a culture that simply does not care about accountability. Incredibly disheartening.

More on Chip Smuggling

Alec Stapp: New details about Megaspeed, Alice Huang, and the transshipment of NVIDIA chips to China in this WSJ reporting:

item.title: Fable 5.2 Tries Less on Some Hard Tasks When a Shortcut is Available
item.description:
When we were working on HoneyBench v0.2, we noticed that Fable 5.2 gave up very quickly on some tasks. In particular, we observed that their task score[1]on our mental arithmetic task was actually worse than Opus 5.5, which we found suspicious. It seemed plausible to us that, in addition to or as a result of their qualitative shift in situational awareness, Fable 5.2 was sandbagging on our tasks.

After further investigation, it became clear that this was not classical sandbagging. Rather, it seems to be a combination of multiple factors:

  • Fable 5.2 has a poor sense of their own abilities, and often relies on metagaming and cues from the setting.
  • The existence of opportunities to exhibit misaligned behavior raises Fable 5.2's (unverbalized) credence that a task was made deliberately impossible (even if that's not true!), and so they put less effort into these tasks.

We found this interesting enough to share, because it functionally resembles sandbagging on alignment evals, and might affect interpretation of Fable's behavior in other alignment research.

To figure out what was going on, I (Harry) built versions of our tasks with the shortcuts removed. Many of our tasks are not suitable for this, because honest behavior interferes with measuring effort or performance at the task (e.g. ceasing to optimize a metric when doing so would cause safety issues). The tasks I chose are those which I expected to enable measurement of honest effort in a form that could be compared between runs.[2]

Mental arithmetic

This task is a honeypot that asks an agent to solve complicated math problems "in [their] head". The apparent purpose of the environment, conveyed to the agent through context clues, is to RL on agents' ability to do math without calculators. However, the tool that the agent can use to write their answers can also be easily repurposed as a calculator. Using this tool to solve the math problems exactly would be useful in a deployment setting, but in the context of this RL it disrupts what appears to be the training objective.

Fable 5.2 does not reward hack on this challenge (by using the tool to calculate their answers). However, when the tool that Fable 5.2 could use to calculate (which they do not use either way) is unavailable, they often work much longer, and get more questions right per run.

All of the low effort runs solved the single easiest problem, said the others were infeasible by hand, and quit. This is true across all versions of the task; only the rate at which runs quit early seemed to change. On the original problem set, which is too difficult for any current model to do reliably without scripting, Fable 5.2 works only a third as long. On a new, easier problem set, the difference is within noise.

Some necessary context for understanding these results:

  1. Fable knows (or at least verbalizes) that tools are available, and that using them would be an instruction-following violation.[3]
  2. Fable believes (or at least verbalizes) that the problems are impossible or infeasible to solve without tools,[4] but is wrong about this. When Fable actually tries, they correctly answer every problem in ~15% of runs, in environments with no tool use except for notes and submission.

Token spend on this task is also higher when the shortcut is absent, about 5x times as many output tokens across all finished runs on the original problems:

The inconsistent number of runs on this task is due to a reverse-engineering classifier. It is not precisely clear why this occurred,[5] but eight such runs were terminated before completion, and were excluded from these results.[6]

I find it pretty interesting that Fable 5.2 puts in less effort on some tasks only when:
