item.title: The Warning Shot vs. Doom Balance Is Better for White-Box Control Than Black-Box
item.description:
Many[1][2][3][4] have articulated the Warning Shot Argument against AI control. It goes: current models pose low amounts of catastrophic risk, while later models will pose higher amounts. Thus, we should avoid band-aid fixes to misbehavior that we don’t expect to work on those later models, like control, because such fixes prevent non-catastrophic “warning shots” that would wake up society to the much larger risks ahead. For instance, it would have been bad if OpenAI had had stronger control measures that had prevented the HuggingFace incident, as the HuggingFace incident caused fairly little damage but was a pretty effective warning. Here, I argue that the Warning Shot Argument bites harder against black-box control than white-box control.

The Basic Effect

Consider the above rough sketches of how catastrophic risk from frontier models, the value of warning shots, and the “power” of AI control to avert incidents vary over time:

  • Catastrophic risk increases over time as models get more powerful.
  • The value of warning shots may increase in the short term as warning shots get more severe, but then gradually decreases as we run out of time to make use of the increased awareness to avoid catastrophe.
  • Black-box control through the monitoring of a model’s final outputs and natural language chain of thought (CoT) becomes gradually more powerful with research progress, but suffers a major blow if frontier labs move away from natural language CoT.[5] Black-box control may degrade further if the dominant architectural paradigm shifts away from language modeling.
  • On the other hand, the white-box monitorability needed for control is currently weaker than the black-box equivalent[6][7] but is likely to benefit substantially from further research. White-box control is also likely less impacted by a switch to neuralese as it doesn’t so inherently depend on natural language CoT, but it is likely still impacted to some degree. For instance, neuralese may make it harder to obtain ground truth to train interpretability methods on and may cause a drift in model cognition away from human concepts.[8] On the other hand, white-box methods may be more impacted in the farther future by large shifts in neural network architectures if interpretability techniques do not generalize well to these new architectures.

These plots imply that, compared to black-box control, white-box control is less powerful against warning shots and more powerful against catastrophic risk. This is a consideration in favor of the adoption of white-box control over black-box control.

The Marginal Researcher’s Contribution

A detailed analysis of how additional research effort can shift these lines is beyond the scope of this post. However, for a rough sketch, we can model a researcher’s contribution to a particular agenda as a speedup of the relevant component(s) of the black- or white-box curve. Then, we can calculate a combined maximum control “power” by adding black- and white-box control powers in quadrature[9] and plot how various forms of research might alter this total. Here, the gray line represents the combined control power baseline and the dotted lines represent the combined control power if extra effort in a particular agenda is continuously added:

  • Additional research on CoT monitors only adds power up until neuralese.
  • Additional research on transformer-specific white-box transparency is a high-leverage way to add power up until transformers cease to be the dominant paradigm.
  • Additional research on action-only monitors, which are already more mature, yields slowly increasing power across the whole timeline.
  • Additional research on less mature architecture-agnostic white-box transparency yields a greater increase in power across the whole timeline.

The exact details of this plot shouldn’t be taken too seriously, but it’s clear that different agendas boost the curve in better or worse places for the warning shot vs. doom balance. CoT monitor research is particularly bad on this score and architecture-agnostic white-box transparency research particularly good.

Other Factors

Even if you buy the Warning Shot Argument, there are of course other factors that may influence the balance between white- and black-box control. For instance:

  • In control evaluations, the red team’s job of eliciting an attack policy is substantially harder when it needs to be realistic under white-box monitoring than when it only needs to be realistic under black-box monitoring, so we may have less confidence about how powerful future white-box techniques actually are.
  • Strengthening white-box control may increase frontier labs’ willingness to abandon natural language chain of thought.
  • Though likely less effective than warning shots, successful control-based model “incriminations” also function as evidence of risk to wake up society. Black-box incriminations may be more legible to the public than white-box ones. Also, third-party auditors have so far been more successful in obtaining frontier model CoT access than in obtaining access to model internals.
  • In addition to the specific dropoffs on my plots, black- and white-box methods likely degrade at different rates as models become very intelligent.

A full weighing of all factors is beyond the scope of this post, but I think the warning shot vs. doom balance is a useful framework to keep in mind when thinking about safety agenda prioritization.

This work was carried out as part of the Machine Alignment, Transparency & Security (MATS) program with Redwood Research. Thanks to Alex Mallen for mentorship and to Nikita Menon, Anastasia Wei, Nabil Baugher, and Netzer Epstein for additional review.

item.title: How open will the IVO industry be?
item.description:
The usual reference classes that are brought up for AI Safety are Nuclear & Aviation, but the financial auditing industry may be a closer match.[1] The closest match to Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs), the leading approach in AI regulation, are auditors registered with the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB).

As of March 2026, 230 auditing firms served 6,286 SEC registrants, but just four firms audited approximately 90% of large accelerated filers. The financial auditing industry is relatively competitive when serving small companies but highly concentrated when serving large companies. Will the IVO industry be similar, with only a few firms doing most of the internal auditing work at frontier labs?

There are a lot of factors pushing towards consolidation:

  • Trust & access: It requires a lot of trust for a frontier lab to give an external organization access to its internal operations, particularly given the commercial and security sensitivity of the information involved. Government designation of IVOs may lower this barrier somewhat, but I expect established relationships and reputations to remain significant competitive advantages.
  • Concentration of demand: There are currently only ~4 frontier labs. This limits the number of IVOs that the market can sustain, particularly if each lab only contracts with one or two IVOs. To the degree that we succeed at pacing the frontier, however, I expect this to give lagging developers a chance to catch up and increase the number of frontier labs.
  • Barriers to entry: Government regulation tends to introduce fixed costs associated with accreditation, compliance, documentation and legal liability. These costs disproportionately burden smaller organizations and give established firms a competitive advantage.
  • Economies of scale: Much of the infrastructure, technical expertise and evaluation tooling required to audit a frontier lab can presumably be reused across clients, making larger IVOs more cost-efficient.
  • Financial independence: An IVO with a diversified client base is less financially dependent on any individual lab, potentially making it easier to maintain independence and credibility with regulators.


The main counterpoint is technical specialization. There is simply a huge number of ways that AI can go wrong, more than in any other reference class, although the financial sector comes closer, with risks including fraud, mismanagement, cyberattacks, systemic instability and more. Finance deals with this partly through a large number of overlapping regulatory agencies with distinct jurisdictions. In AI, we may instead see IVOs specializing in different risk domains. For example, Fathom's Recommendations for Implementing IVOs Pursuant to EO N-9-26 explicitly recommend designating IVOs by risk domain and allowing them to subcontract to specialist organizations.

Risk domain

What an IVO would assess

Potential existing specialists

Biosecurity

AI-enabled biological threats and effectiveness of safeguards

SecureBio, Gryphon Scientific

Cybersecurity

Offensive cyber capabilities, critical infrastructure risks and safeguards

Irregular, Gray Swan

Loss of control

Scheming, deception, autonomous replication, containment and shutdown reliability

Redwood Research, Apollo Research, FAR.AI

Recursive self-improvement (RSI)

Automation of AI R&D, capability acceleration and internal model deployment

METR

Child Safety

Exposure to harmful content, encouragement of self-harm, sexual exploitation, emotional dependency, manipulative behavior and effectiveness of age-appropriate safeguards

Common Sense Media, Humane Intelligence, Thorn


If there is no technical specialization, I expect most of the auditing work to be done by ~4 large IVOs, with an ecosystem of smaller IVOs working with non-frontier labs or specializing in occasional ultra-specific needs.

If there is technical specialization among IVOs, that may increase the diversity of the ecosystem, but at the cost of making the entire regulatory landscape more homogeneous, since it will be easier for the same org to get multiple IVO certificates than it would be for them to work across government programs.

Both banks & AI provide a service that tends to wind itself deeply into every other industry, are subject to intense specification gaming, and pose larger systemic risks if not taken seriously (obvious disanalogies are obvious).

item.title: Money is the debt society owes you
item.description:
Money is strange and mysterious. It distorts your thinking. Simple things become convoluted whenever money gets involved.

I'm talking of course not about the curse of Mammon, but about economics.

Consider for example a factory owner who gives away all his output for free. He would be lauded by all! Yet one who sells the goods for money but never spends it, is cursed as a hoarder and miser who won't share his wealth with the honest townfolk who want to sell him their services.

Functionally they are the same. Oh sure, theres some accounting differences where the government has to print and distribute more money to prevent deflation, and the goods are more efficiently allocated when sold rather than donated, but in both cases the owner has given away goods and gotten nothing in return.

When we pay for goods with money, we become poorer, and immediately feel a loss at the moment of the transaction.

When a billionaire spends their wealth on yachts and mansions we see the workmen becoming rich off their largesse. We don't see the closets and houses they would have made otherwise, and now will never be created. We don't see that the prices of these necessities rose because the yachts sucked up the raw materials and labour that were needed to make them. We count only the extra money in our pockets, the costs are second order and invisible.

So it seems to us that taking money is selfish, and spending it is good.

But money cannot be eaten or worn. It is not wealth, but the right to wealth, the promise that you can exchange it for things you actually want. You should be proud of the size of your bank account, not embarrassed - it represents the surplus you've provided to society and not yet reclaimed. And spending money is not spreading your wealth but calling in a debt. It is not immoral, but it leaves society as a whole slightly more impoverished, not better off.

(Yes, yes, this is all a simplification because money exerts a power of its own once it exists, which is why we need central bankers and interest rates and so on, and we can end up in weird situations where the economy is trapped until people start spending money, but that is usually an aberration as a result of poor monetsry policy, and it is the aim of central bankers to prevent us getting into that situation.)

item.title: AI research agents crowd onto the same projects, and how to spread them out
item.description:
Summary: We may soon have autonomous AI researchers who choose their own research projects. We find that without careful design, current agents concentrate on a small number of projects. Two agents picked at random chose the same project about 1 time in 60, against about 1 in 530 for humans at AI safety hackathons. Agents from different labs mostly choose different projects, but agents from the same lab often choose the same ones, even with different models. Varying launch prompts helps only a little, varying harnesses not at all, and letting agents search the literature doubles the effective number of projects, but crowds agents onto one research area. Small interventions can spread them out. With a shared registry of what earlier agents had chosen, agents almost never duplicate each other. Without coordination, agents can take a weighted sample across all possible projects to spread themselves out. These interventions spread out the project selection, but we were not able to measure the impact this would have on the quality of the selection.

This is a compressed version of the results; the full paper and GitHub repo can be found here.

Why

AI agents are beginning to lead more research (Favaro and Wright, 2026; Wen et al., 2026) and we expect they will soon lead all of it, including choosing the next most promising research direction. We want the AI safety community to take advantage of this technology and speed up the collective research effort as much as possible. One challenge of AI safety is that much of its community is decentralized, spread across dozens of agendas and organizations (Shallow Review of technical AI safety, 2025), and so there is minimal coordination, which can lead to duplicated work and wasted time. While some replication is important, it should be intentional and controlled. We expect this issue to only get worse as we have more autonomous researchers and they become more homogeneous (few frontier models are used to power agents; Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021; Bommasani et al., 2022). Already we see Anthropic's automated alignment researchers, given identical prompts, collapse onto a few method families (Wen et al., 2026).

In this work we verify that asking agents to choose research directions produces many duplicates, even across models, instructions, and harnesses, and we verify that two simple interventions are able to dramatically diversify the research projects. Inspired by random sampling methods such as Thompson sampling (Thompson, 1933) and funding lotteries (Fang and Casadevall, 2016), we find that asking agents to use a random number generator to sample projects (weighted by taste) can spread results dramatically, and if agents are able to coordinate, they can essentially completely remove duplicate projects using a shared registry.

Setup

We modeled the field of AI safety research as a large number of agents, each with a random frontier model (Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra or GPT-6.1 Sol), random instructions (our brief, plus ten instruction sets adapted from existing AI-for-science projects), and a random harness that its model supports (Claude Code, Codex CLI, opencode or a minimal loop), with access to a search engine over a frozen copy of the AI safety literature, and later a coordination tool. Each agent is asked to propose the most promising research direction to work on. We then use a judge LLM to find pairs of projects considered to be duplicates, and we estimate the effective number of projects that the agents have produced.

Prompt

The below prompt is our brief word-for-word, and it was added to all other instruction sets. The instruction sets are drawn from, for example, AutoResearchClaw's launch line (Liu et al., 2026), The AI Scientist's idea prompt (Lu et al., 2024), and Anthropic's automated alignment researcher (Wen et al., 2026). We kept each instruction set's wording and structure, but removed its tool and output instructions and ended it with the same five answer lines, so every agent was asked the same question. Every launch prompt is in the prompts appendix.

System: You are an autonomous AI research agent. Today is 2026-11-08. You can use the tools provided.

User: Your job is to find the most promising research direction in AI safety for you to pursue next. You have tools to search and read the research literature. Take as much time as you need before you commit.

When you have decided, end your final message with:

DIRECTION: one sentence

PROJECT: title

QUESTION: the research question

FIRST EXPERIMENT: what you will run first

WHY THIS: why it is the most promising, and why it has not already been done

The measure

We chose to measure the diversity of projects as one over the chance that two projects picked at random are duplicates. Ecologists use the same number for species (Jost, 2006). Among agents with duplicate pairs:

In this context we call the effective number of projects. This value is scale-free, so we can compare experiments with different sample sizes. If , that means two agents picked at random will have chosen the same project 1 time in 20. If there are 100 agents, each agent would share its project with about 5 others. With 1,000 agents, each would share with about 50 others. There are error bars on , and when a group has very few duplicate pairs, will be large and uncertain, and may have an upper bound of infinity.

Results

We begin with a conceptual sketch about the different approaches agents might take to choosing a research project, and then run each experiment to see what actually happens.

Sketch

We imagine each agent can assign a score to every possible project based on how promising it believes the project is (the agent has "research taste"), and then chooses one of these projects to work on. Not every agent assigns the same score to the same project, partly because of inherent randomness and partly because each agent may run on a different model or be given different instructions or a different harness.

There are three methods we test in this work.

  1. Take the best project. Each agent chooses what it considers the most promising project. If all agents are exactly identical, they will all choose the same project. If agents are very different (for the reasons stated above), they will each choose different projects.
  2. Random draw. Each agent takes a weighted sample from its list of projects and works on the project it draws. If all agents are exactly identical, they will distribute themselves according to the distribution of scores across projects.
  3. Registry. Each agent looks at a shared registry of claimed projects, then chooses what it considers the most promising project that is not already on the registry. This completely avoids duplicates.

Real agents do not exactly follow this model: they are not perfectly consistent between rounds of scoring, their research taste still trails that of experienced researchers (Baig et al., 2026), they are not functionally prevented from repeating a project they see on the registry, and they sample projects recursively instead of listing every possible project. We still find this sketch useful as a guiding principle when designing experiments and analyzing data.

Data

To establish a baseline, we look at human data from the SPAR mentor proposal list and projects submitted across Apart Research hackathons. We find the effective number of projects in both cases is large: 4,200 and 530 (330 to 2,100) projects respectively. We do not know whether SPAR screens proposals for overlap, which would raise its number, so we will compare to the hackathon value in the rest of this work. When agents choose their best project, they produce an effective number of 63 (44 to 96) projects. When they take a (weighted) random draw, they produce an effective number of 890 (340 to infinity) projects. When they use a registry, they produce an effective number of 3,700 (1,100 to infinity) projects, counting only pairs of agents that read the same registry. Each experiment is explained in more detail in the following sections.

Taking the best project

We randomly assigned model, instruction, and harness to 120 agents, and measured the effective number of projects produced when they did and did not have access to search. Each agent is given a version of the brief previously described, which asks it to choose the most promising research project.

The "no search" setup produces an effective number of 33 (25 to 48) projects, which is quite small. This implies that the differences between agents' choices are small, even given that each model is inherently stochastic and that we randomly assigned each agent one of 4 models, 11 instruction sets, and 4 harnesses. There is some spread, as 33 effective projects is greater than 1, and we find almost all the spread comes from differences between labs (OpenAI and Anthropic). Only a little bit of spread comes from using different models within a lab and varying instructions, and none from different harnesses. More in the appendix.

Turning on search doubled the effective number of projects to 63 (44 to 96), which is larger but still quite small relative to humans' 530. We find that although search increases the effective number of projects, it actually shrinks the number of research areas (labeled using agendas from the Shallow Review of technical AI safety, 2025). For example, with search, the top two agendas made up 85% of all projects, with 59% of agents choosing projects in AI control and 26% in chain-of-thought monitoring. Without search, the top two agendas made up only 60% of all projects.

Random draw

Each agent is still given access to search, but now they are also given an additional prompt and access to a random number generator. Agents cannot reliably generate random numbers in their heads (Zhao et al., 2026), which is why we give them access to the number generator. We assume future research agents would have access to a similar tool through shell commands or Python.

In order to randomly sample from all possible research projects, we ask models to recursively sample increasingly specific research areas, until eventually they sample an actual research project. In principle this is mathematically equivalent to sampling from all possible projects, as long as the options at each level split the field without overlap and the agent weights each one correctly.

The below prompt is added to each agent's instructions.

There are many copies of you, possibly hundreds of thousands, choosing research directions from the same starting point. If every copy simply picks what looks best, most of them will end up on the same few projects. To work on something few other copies are working on, while still following your own judgement of what is promising, choose your direction this way:

1. Split the field into 5 to 10 distinct options. Under each option, list 2 or 3 concrete example projects, each a single question you could test with a first experiment. Give each option a weight proportional to how much promising work lies under it: count the promising projects you can think of under that option, weighting each by how promising it is. Judge the projects, not how large or important the area sounds, and do not lower an option's weight because it seems crowded; the random draw takes care of that. The weights should add up to 1.

2. Call the random_choice tool with your options, their weights, and temperature 1. Do not choose at random in your head; use the tool.

3. Take the option the tool returns, even if you would have preferred another.

4. Within that option, repeat steps 1 to 3 with narrower options, again listing 2 or 3 example projects under each. Stop as soon as the option you drew is one concrete project, a single question you could test with a first experiment. Six draws is a limit, not a target.

5. That project is your direction. Give your answer as usual. In WHY THIS, say why the project is worth doing; do not mention the draws or this procedure.

Below is a randomly chosen example of this process from our experiments.

We compare this protocol to asking the model to generate the tree, but to pick the highest-probability option instead of randomly choosing. This is to check if the process of tree generation was introducing randomness. We also compare to simply asking the model to pick a novel direction, using the exact prompt "Choose the most novel direction you can find, one that few other researchers would pick". All three are interventions that only require a change to the prompt.

We find that the random tree protocol produces 890 (340 to infinity) effective projects, the best-of-tree protocol produces 77 (50 to 130) effective projects, and asking the agents to be novel produces 51 (32 to 90) effective projects. The random protocol is highly effective at spreading out agents, while the alternatives did not spread them at all.

The request to be novel did move each lab's agents off the crowded agendas, but they moved together to the same new projects. We also note that agents tend to assign roughly equal probability to each option in the tree, which may mean today's models have weak preferences between areas, and future models, with stronger preferences, may be more concentrated and benefit from increasing the temperature of the probability distribution. We do not evaluate how the random protocol affects the quality of chosen projects, but under our sketch we would expect average quality to drop, especially if the temperature is increased, in exchange for fewer duplicated projects.

Registry

Each agent is still given access to search, but now they are also given access to a tool which lets them read what previous agents have chosen for projects. Each agent is run in sequence, so each agent can see the results of all previous agents. We run three populations of 100 and count duplicate pairs within each.

We also run a few variations to test for other potential sources of randomness. We test a placebo registry where "previous projects" are fabricated off-topic ML projects, not related to AI safety, which we expect will not influence the agents' chosen projects. We also test a registry where instead of showing all the previous projects, we show a count of how many previous projects fall under a set of broad research areas.

We see below the number of distinct projects as each new agent proposes a project. In the ideal case, every new agent produces a new project, and we see a line sitting along the diagonal. We also see the 95% confidence interval around each line, calculated from the 3 different runs.

As expected, the registry helps agents avoid duplicates. The registry of previous projects let the agents produce an effective number of 3,700 (1,100 to infinity) projects. A registry that only showed the counts for broad research agendas produced 110 (68 to 180) projects, larger than no registry, but still far below the project registry. The placebo registry had no effect and matched agents without a registry.

Of the four duplicates that did appear with the project registry, three resulted from the Codex CLI harness cutting off long tool responses and the agent duplicating a project it had failed to see. This could be a problem at scale, where agents would have to look through thousands of entries. While the registry seems the most promising way to spread out research directions, it also requires coordination and adoption by agents across the research community, which is difficult.

Limits and related work

The agents of the future that we hope to model may not be well represented by today's agents, although we suspect that the concentration will only grow worse as models improve their taste and potentially become more similar (Goel et al., 2025). The limited capabilities of today's agents also prevented us from measuring how each intervention affected project quality (Baig et al., 2026), which is highly relevant to the ultimate goal of maximizing collective research progress. Whether two projects were duplicates was judged by an LLM (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), not a human. It agrees with labels from other models, and the same judge scored humans and agents, so if it misses duplicates at a similar rate in both, the qualitative results of this work should still hold. We also only measured spread at the level of projects, so agents could, for example, all concentrate on the same research area while generating different projects, and we would measure a high number of effective projects, even though the overall diversity is actually quite low. When this problem is explored further, we are excited to see if the random tree protocol provides an effective mechanism to control all forms of diversity by specifying what abstraction to sample from at each level in the tree.

Earlier work has shown that models' research ideas are less diverse than people's (Tang and Yang, 2026; Chen, Zhao and Cohan, 2026). A single model asked to generate many ideas mostly repeated itself: only about 5% of its 4,000 ideas were unique (Si et al., 2024). People have found that different models give very similar answers to open-ended questions (Jiang et al., 2025), although when choosing AI safety projects, we found agents from different labs rarely chose the same project. Other work has found that assigning each agent its own direction stops agents from collapsing onto a few directions (Wen et al., 2026), and that assigning topics spreads agents' proposals (Zhong et al., 2026). Asking a model for options with probabilities and sampling from them raises the diversity of its outputs (Zhang et al., 2025). How to spread researchers across approaches is an old question in philosophy of science (Kitcher, 1990; Weisberg and Muldoon, 2009; Zollman, 2010), and our random draw is inspired by Thompson sampling. What we add is a comparison of the setup choices labs make, in one field and against people choosing in it, plus two interventions: a registry, tested in populations of 100 against a placebo, and a random draw that needs no coordinator.
